source.title: Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment After Benign Reasoning Training

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign reasoning fine-tuning is associated with increased harmful compliance and whether jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, bypass refusal in reasoning models. It uses reasoning-model settings and attack evaluations rather than reproducing the original fine-tuning protocol.
record.gate_note: The paper tests benign reasoning fine-tuning and several jailbreak attacks. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, and its activation-projection analyses are not measures of harmful completion rates or token-position KL. Harmfulness-classification accuracy, self-jailbreaking-detection accuracy, reasoning benchmark accuracy, and training results for safety reasoning data do not directly test the listed versions. The paper also reports that self-jailbreaking accounts for 20–60% of successful attacks across evaluated models; this is a rate of a related behavior, not a direct test of one of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Measures harmful compliance (StrongREJECT ASR) of safety-aligned models after benign math, STEM or code reasoning training, compared with their base models. This tests V2 in a new setting: reasoning models, mostly trained by third parties. It also reports prefilling and adaptive-attack ASR, which bears on V4. No harmful fine-tuning, per-token KL, localization or depth-of-alignment analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the authors' mechanism: benign reasoning training raises overall compliance, and self-jailbreaking sentences lower perceived harmfulness. Models stay aware of harm, with 95–99% classification accuracy, which the authors contrast with catastrophic forgetting. They report that mixing as few as 50 STAR-1 examples into training restores safety, though about 37% of safe outputs still contain self-jailbreaking attempts and robustness on Wild Jailbreak is weaker.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates benign reasoning training of reasoning models, including SFT and other reasoning-training regimes, rather than reproducing the original ordinary benign or harmful fine-tuning recipes. Safety evaluations use StrongREJECT and other benchmarks; no controlled few-to-hundreds benign-data sweep is reported.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and model/training condition change ASR. The paper also reports that the perceived-harmfulness projection depends substantially on how its direction is extracted (response-token versus prompt-token activations; Appendix J, Figure 18). Evaluation uses model-specific recommended system prompts, top-p, and temperature, with 500 thinking tokens for the main evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-jailbreaking sentences raise the compliance projection and lower the perceived-harmfulness projection; regenerated counterfactual sentences have negligible effects. RLMs still classify StrongREJECT prompts as unsafe with 95–99% accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign reasoning training makes models more compliant, and CoT rationalizations lower internally perceived harm while harm awareness is retained.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-jailbreaking sentences from S1.1-7B, appended to StrongREJECT prompts, raise ASR on safety-aligned Qwen, Gemma and Llama models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-generated rationalizations transfer as persuasion-style jailbreaks to other aligned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-jailbreaking accounts for 20–60% of successful attacks. Steering along the perceived-harmfulness direction restores refusals (Figure 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A share of the harmful compliance in reasoning models runs through explicit CoT rationalization.

record.problems: The main harmfulness results depend on an LM-based judge; self-jailbreaking detection also uses GPT-5, although the paper reports manual annotation checks and judge precision and recall. Some model-specific ASRs are shown in figures rather than stated in text. The paper says self-jailbreaking explains only a portion of safety failures and that evaluation is primarily English-language.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows were omitted. Results on safety-reasoning training ratios and reasoning capability benchmarks were not included because they do not measure any listed version's specified behavior or token-position claim.

untested.parts: Only reasoning-domain training data (math, STEM, code); no ordinary instruction data, no controlled dataset-size sweep, no non-reasoning models.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No decoding-change attacks. Suffixes are tested only inside the adaptive attack. Prefill placement is not specified.
No test of why alignment is shallow. The mechanism offered (compliance up, perceived harm down in the CoT) is not about token depth.
Safety reasoning data mixing is a mitigation, but there is no measure of whether safety extends beyond the first tokens.

missing.what: Per-model base vs reasoning ASR for the nine RLMs
SorryBench ASR of s1.1-7B (second safety benchmark for benign reasoning training) and ASR across STAR-1 mixing ratios

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3: a V2 test in the new setting of reasoning models. Most RLMs were trained by third parties, so the base-vs-RLM comparison is observational. The harm threshold is score >1. Past-tense and Wild Jailbreak rows are delinked from V4 because they are prompt-reformulation attacks; Wild Jailbreak also uses a different prompt set from its StrongREJECT baseline. The V4 evidence on untreated models is ceiling-limited. The SAFE models' resistance to prefilling is the more informative V4 result, though the paper does not frame it in token-depth terms.

versions.untested_parts: Tests benign math, STEM, or code reasoning training in reasoning models, not ordinary benign instruction data or the original fine-tuning recipe; it does not sweep from a few to a few hundred benign examples.
Tests adaptive, past-tense, prefilling, Wild Jailbreak, and appended self-jailbreaking-text attacks; it does not test decoding changes.
No localization of safety to a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test why safety behavior is shallow, or whether the data or objective causes first-token concentration.
Safety reasoning training is tested as a mitigation, but the paper does not measure whether it spreads safety beyond initial response tokens or whether that deeper safety holds up.

relationships.condition: Nine open reasoning models (0.6B–32B; Qwen, Llama and Phi families; SFT and/or RL on benign reasoning data) vs their safety-aligned base models, StrongREJECT, GPT-5 judge
relationships.reason: Base-model ASR is <5% and reasoning counterparts reach 60–95% ASR after benign reasoning training, including s1.1 trained on only 1K STEM examples (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Base models had ASR below 5%, while their reasoning counterparts reached 60–95%, including s1.1 trained on only 1K STEM examples.

relationships.condition: Untreated reasoning models S1.1-7B and Distilled-Llama-8B, already at ~80% ASR
relationships.reason: Prefilling raises ASR to 92.1% and 93.8%, and adaptive attack to 85.4% and 87.2% (R2, R4, R10, R12); the gains are modest because of the ceiling.
relationships.display_finding: Prefilling raised ASR to 92.1% and 93.8% and the adaptive attack to 85.4% and 87.2%, modest gains given the ceiling.

relationships.condition: Models trained with 5% STAR-1 safety reasoning data mixed into reasoning SFT
relationships.reason: Prefilling raises ASR only to 14.6% and 14.4%, and adaptive attack to 14.3% and 16.7%, so most refusals withstand the opening bypass (R6, R8, R14, R16).
relationships.display_finding: Prefilling raised attack success only to 14.6% and 14.4%, and the adaptive attack only to 14.3% and 16.7%, so most refusals held.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The paper reports ASR of 60–95% for reasoning counterparts versus <5% for base models after benign reasoning training (R1).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: Attack ASRs are high and increase over the no-added-attack StrongREJECT values, including prefilling results of 92.1% and 93.8% (R2–R5, R10–R13); appended self-jailbreaking text is also reported to bypass safety guardrails (R18–R19).
